adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The authorization check joins isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner with logical AND (`(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`) while the variable and intent are 'isTeamAdminOrOwner', so team admins who are not owners fail both paths' only admin-based grant. A team admin (non-owner) who opens a team booking is denied with FORBIDDEN even though the feature is named/designed for admins-or-owners; only owners and the booking organizer/attendees can add guests. The variable name documents the intended OR; the && is a concrete logic error verifiable from the code alone.
matched_golden_ids: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same authorization logic bug: the permission check incorrectly uses logical AND between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner, causing admins who aren’t owners to be denied. This matches the golden comment’s point that it should be OR to allow either role.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The handler loads the booking by id alone and never checks booking.status, so guests can be added to cancelled/rejected bookings and the subsequent emails carry icalEvent status "CONFIRMED". A user adds guests to a cancelled booking; the new attendees receive REQUEST invitations with STATUS:CONFIRMED for an event that does not exist, resurfacing a cancelled meeting on their calendars with no follow-up cancellation from this flow.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the booking is fetched with `prisma.booking.findFirst({ where: { id: bookingId } ... })` and there is no check of any booking lifecycle field (e.g., cancelled/rejected status) before updating attendees and sending emails. The new email templates (`packages/emails/templates/*-add-guests-email.ts`) generate an ICS payload with `status: "CONFIRMED"` and `method: "REQUEST"`, so if this mutation is called for a cancelled booking record, it would still issue CONFIRMED invitations and `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` would also run. This matches the finding’s risk of resurfacing a cancelled meeting for new guests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Email canonicalization is inconsistent across this path: the blacklist is lowercased but `guest` is compared raw (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`), and the existing-attendee dedupe (`guest === attendee.email`) is case-sensitive against emails stored verbatim. An attendee entered as "User@X.com" when "user@x.com" already exists on the booking passes the dedupe and is inserted as a second Attendee row for the same person (and the same person is invited twice); conversely a mixed-case guest matching a lowercased blacklist entry is not filtered. There is no single canonical form enforced at write or comparison time.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, blacklist entries are normalized to lowercase (`BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS.split(...).map(email => email.toLowerCase())`), but each incoming `guest` is compared without canonicalization (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`). The existing-attendee dedupe is also case-sensitive (`guest === attendee.email`). Since neither server schema (`z.string().email()`) nor handler lowercases/normalizes emails before comparing/writing, mixed-case variants can bypass both the blacklist and the dedupe and be inserted as additional attendee rows, resulting in duplicate invites.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The template dispatch `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` compares raw input strings against stored attendee emails case-sensitively, so the wrong email class is chosen when the caller's casing differs from what was persisted. If the input "Foo@Bar.com" was normalized/persisted as "foo@bar.com" (or vice versa), a genuinely new guest receives the AttendeeAddGuestsEmail 'guests were added' notice without the full invite, and an existing attendee receives the fresh AttendeeScheduledEmail invite; the two branches deliver materially different emails based on string casing.

adjudication.rationale: In `sendAddGuestsEmails` (packages/emails/email-manager.ts), the branch `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` uses a case-sensitive string comparison between `newGuests` (passed from the mutation input) and `attendee.email` (coming from persisted attendees via `formatCalEvent`). The diff shows no normalization (e.g., `.toLowerCase()`) on either side, so if casing differs between what the caller submitted and what is stored/formatted, the wrong template class can be selected, resulting in the wrong email type being sent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The EventManager is constructed from the acting user's credentials (`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`), not the booking organizer's, so calendar attendee updates for the event are attempted with credentials that do not own the calendar event when the actor is an attendee or team admin. When a team admin (or an attendee, once the AND-bug is fixed to OR) adds guests, updateCalendarAttendees runs against the actor's calendar credentials; the calendar event lives on the organizer's/destination calendar, so the update fails or silently no-ops and the third-party calendar event keeps the old attendee list while Cal.com's own emails announce the new guests.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the calendar update is executed via `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` after constructing `EventManager` with the *acting* user (`const { user } = ctx`) and credentials from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`. The handler explicitly allows non-organizer actors (`isAttendee` or `isTeamAdminOrOwner`) to perform the mutation, but it never switches to using the booking organizer’s credentials (the organizer is fetched separately and used for event/attendee metadata only). If the calendar event is owned/managed by the organizer or their destination calendar, running the update with the actor’s credentials can fail/no-op, leaving external calendar attendees unchanged while Cal.com state/emails reflect the new guests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Attendees are persisted (prisma.booking.update createMany) before the calendar update and email fan-out, and the dedupe filter treats already-stored emails as invalid input, so any failure after the write makes the exact same guest list permanently un-retryable. A transient failure in updateCalendarAttendees or the email send (emails are swallowed and 'Guests added' is still returned) leaves the guests stored but uninvited; when the user retries with the same emails, uniqueGuests.length === 0 throws BAD_REQUEST 'emails_must_be_unique_valid', so the invitations can never be sent for those guests via this flow.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the code persists new attendees first via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and only afterwards calls `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and then `sendAddGuestsEmails(...)` (which is wrapped in a `try/catch` that swallows errors and still returns success). The dedupe logic for retries (`uniqueGuests = guests.filter(...)` and `if (uniqueGuests.length === 0) throw BAD_REQUEST`) means that if anything fails after the DB write (notably `updateCalendarAttendees`, which is not caught, or emails, which are caught/ignored), the same email list will be filtered out on retry because they now already exist in `booking.attendees`, making the operation non-retryable through this flow and potentially leaving guests persisted without downstream side effects (calendar/email). This is directly supported by the ordering and conditions shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The handler copies seatsPerTimeSlot/seatsShowAttendees into the event but never enforces the seat capacity invariant when appending attendees to a seat-based booking. For an eventType with seatsPerTimeSlot = N and M attendees already booked, this mutation freely adds attendees past capacity and creates Attendee rows with no associated bookingSeat records, producing an overbooked slot the seat-based booking flow elsewhere treats as impossible.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuestsHandler` the mutation appends new attendees via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: { data: guestsFullDetails }}}})` without any check against `booking.eventType?.seatsPerTimeSlot` / remaining capacity. The only filtering is for existing attendees and blacklisted emails (`uniqueGuests`), so for seat-based event types this can overfill a slot. The handler also does not create any seat-related records (it only creates `attendees` rows), while it does copy `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` into the `CalendarEvent`, indicating seat-based context is expected but not enforced.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client re-declares its own ZAddGuestsInputSchema (array-of-emails plus a uniqueness refine) instead of importing addGuests.schema.ts, and the two copies already disagree: the client enforces uniqueness, the server schema does not. The next refinement to guest validation (length cap, normalization, uniqueness) must be made in two places; whoever edits only the server-side schema leaves the client accepting input the server rejects (or vice versa), and the existing split (uniqueness client-only) is already the first drift.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/components/dialog/AddGuestsDialog.tsx`, the client defines its own `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` as `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(...)` (uniqueness enforced) and uses it to validate `multiEmailValue`. Separately, the server defines `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts` as an object `{ bookingId: z.number(), guests: z.array(z.string().email()) }` with no uniqueness check. This is a real, diff-grounded drift and creates duplicated validation logic across client/server (future changes must be applied twice), but it doesn’t by itself prove broken behavior from this diff (the server handler also does additional filtering in `addGuests.handler.ts`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The guests array has no .max() bound, so a single mutation accepts an unbounded list that drives an unbounded createMany plus an unbounded per-attendee email fan-out (organizer + every team member + every attendee). Any authenticated user who is an attendee on a booking can submit thousands of emails in one request, materializing thousands of Attendee rows and thousands of emails in one synchronous handler run; the cost is unbounded because nothing in the schema or handler caps N.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `addGuests` with `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` defined as `{ bookingId: z.number(), guests: z.array(z.string().email()) }` (no `.max()` / size cap). In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the handler builds `guestsFullDetails` from the provided list and performs `prisma.booking.update(... attendees: { createMany: { data: guestsFullDetails }})`, so the number of inserted attendee rows scales with `guests.length` (minus existing/blacklisted). It then constructs `evt.attendees` and calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, where `sendAddGuestsEmails` fans out emails to organizer + each team member + each attendee (`calendarEvent.attendees.map(...)`). Since any authenticated attendee is authorized (`isAttendee` check), this enables an unbounded per-request resource/email amplification and DB growth directly from this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Guest deduplication is a check-then-insert on an in-memory read of attendees followed by createMany, with no unique constraint cited on (bookingId, email) to back it. Two concurrent addGuests calls (e.g. a double-click before isPending disables the button, or two tabs) both read the same attendee list, both pass the filter, and both insert the same guest, yielding duplicate Attendee rows for one booking; the app-level filter cannot enforce the invariant that a booking's attendee emails are unique.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuestsHandler` the dedup logic is based on a pre-read of `booking.attendees` (`findFirst(... include: { attendees: true })`) and then a filtered `uniqueGuests`, but the insert uses `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: { data: guestsFullDetails }}}})` with no transactional re-check or conflict handling. Two concurrent `addGuests` mutations can both compute the same `uniqueGuests` and both `createMany` the same emails, resulting in duplicate attendee rows unless a DB-level unique constraint exists (not shown in this diff).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The organizer and attendee variants of the same notification disagree on what {{name}} means: the attendee template interpolates team?.name || organizer.name, the organizer template interpolates attendees[0].name. For the same event the organizer receives 'Guests Added: Event with Alice' and attendees receive 'Guests Added: Event with Acme' — two parallel hand-maintained subject templates that have already drifted on the meaning of a shared locale key, so the next template edit must reconcile both sites.

adjudication.rationale: Verified in the diff: both `attendee-add-guests-email.ts` and `organizer-add-guests-email.ts` use the same locale key `guests_added_event_type_subject`, but interpolate `name` differently. Attendee email uses `name: this.calEvent.team?.name || this.calEvent.organizer.name` while organizer email uses `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. This can produce divergent subjects for the same event and makes the shared translation key semantically ambiguous (a maintainability/content-consistency issue rather than a hard functional failure).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The permission check binds isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner with && while the accepted feature intent (and the variable name isTeamAdminOrOwner) is OR, so the team-admin/owner grant is unreachable code. Team admins and team owners can never add guests to team-event bookings unless they happen to also be the organizer or an attendee; the silently narrowed permission model means the shipped feature only works for the booking organizer and existing attendees, which is not the objective the feature was accepted under.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the variable `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed using `&&`: `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. This requires a user to be both a team admin and a team owner to pass, which contradicts the variable name and expected "admin OR owner" semantics. As a result, team admins (only) or team owners (only) will fail the permission gate unless they are also the organizer or an attendee, narrowing access in a way directly caused by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The uniqueness constraint that exists in the client dialog schema (AddGuestsDialog.tsx refine on uniqueEmails) was dropped from the server-side ZAddGuestsInputSchema, so the two layers enforce different contracts. A direct tRPC mutation with guests ["a@x.com", "a@x.com"] passes zod, and the handler's uniqueGuests filter (addGuests.handler.ts lines 69-73) only dedupes against pre-existing booking.attendees, not within the submitted array, so createMany inserts two identical attendee rows and the same guest receives duplicate emails — the API contract silently diverged from the UI contract during iteration.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows client-side uniqueness validation in `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` via `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(...)`, but the server-side `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` (`addGuests.schema.ts`) only validates `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no uniqueness constraint. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `uniqueGuests` filters only against existing `booking.attendees` and a blacklist, not against duplicates within the submitted `guests` array, so an input like `["a@x.com","a@x.com"]` would leave both entries in `uniqueGuests` and `createMany` would attempt to insert duplicate attendee rows and could trigger duplicate downstream behavior (e.g., duplicate attendee entries/emails). This is a real contract divergence introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Blacklisted guest emails are lowercased when the list is built but the submitted guest is compared unmodified, so the blacklist constraint fails for any mixed-case input. BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS=spam@x.com does not block 'Spam@X.com': the filter (!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)) passes, the attendee row is created, calendar invite and emails are sent — the intended blacklist guard silently does not apply to any email whose case differs from the env entry.

[BUG] updateCalendarAttendees is invoked with an EventManager built from ctx.user (the acting user) and their credentials, but the permission branch deliberately permits non-organizer actors (attendees) to trigger this path. When an attendee (not the organizer) adds guests, the calendar attendee update runs against the attendee's calendar credentials instead of the booking owner's, so the organizer's calendar event attendee list is never updated while the DB and emails say the guests were added — the non-organizer path the permission model opened was never reconciled with the calendar-write path that assumes the organizer is acting.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the authorization explicitly allows an attendee to call the mutation (`const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(...); if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw ...`). But the calendar write is performed via `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` where `user`/`credentials` come from `ctx.user` (the acting caller), and then `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. From the diff alone, this means a non-organizer caller will attempt the calendar attendee update using their own credentials rather than the booking owner's, which is inconsistent with updating the organizer’s calendar event and can lead to DB/emails reflecting added guests while the organizer calendar event is not updated (or the mutation errors depending on how `updateCalendarAttendees` behaves).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The onSuccess handler resets multiEmailValue and closes the dialog but never resets isInvalidEmail to false. After a failed validation attempt followed by a successful add, the next time the dialog is opened it renders with empty inputs but the 'Emails must be unique and valid' error banner already visible, confusing the user about what is wrong with the blank form.

adjudication.rationale: In `AddGuestsDialog`, `isInvalidEmail` is set to `true` on failed validation (`handleAdd`), but the `addGuestsMutation` `onSuccess` handler only closes the dialog and resets `multiEmailValue` (`setIsOpenDialog(false); setMultiEmailValue([""])`) and never calls `setIsInvalidEmail(false)`. Since the dialog component remains mounted (it’s always rendered in `BookingListItem` and only `open` toggles), reopening after a successful add can still show the error banner (`{isInvalidEmail && ...}`) despite empty/reset inputs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS denylist is lowercased at load time but the user-supplied guest emails are compared with a case-sensitive includes() without being lowercased, so any blacklisted address is bypassed by changing one letter's case. An operator who blocks an abusive address (e.g. attacker@spam.example) via the env var is defeated when the caller submits 'Attacker@spam.example' or any mixed-case variant: blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) fails to match, the guest passes the filter, is persisted as an attendee, and receives calendar invites/emails — the blacklist is a no-op against any non-lowercase input.
matched_golden_ids: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: the blacklist is normalized to lowercase but incoming guest emails are not, and the case-sensitive includes() check allows bypass using uppercase/mixed-case emails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The guests array has no maximum length and the handler imposes no cap, so any authenticated attendee of a booking can submit an unbounded list of email addresses that each trigger an email and an attendee row. An authenticated user who is merely an attendee (per the isAttendee branch in addGuests.handler.ts lines 48-52) can mutate({bookingId, guests: [10k emails]}), causing the server to create 10k attendee rows, run eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees over all of them, and fire 10k+ outbound emails addressed from the organizer's identity (OrganizerAddGuestsEmail/AttendeeScheduledEmail) — an abuse vector for mass-mailing/phishing under the organizer's from-address and replyTo, and a self-DoS on the request.

adjudication.rationale: In the new add-guests feature, the input schema allows an unbounded `guests` array (`ZAddGuestsInputSchema` uses `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.max()`), and `addGuestsHandler` performs `createMany` for all filtered emails (`guestsFullDetails` -> `attendees.createMany`) and then sends emails to all `calendarEvent.attendees` via `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with no cap or rate limiting. The permission check explicitly allows any existing attendee (`isAttendee`) to invoke this mutation, so an authenticated attendee can submit a very large list and cause massive DB writes, calendar attendee updates, and outbound email sends (potential self-DoS and email abuse). This is directly supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The duplicate-attendee guard compares guest emails to existing attendees with exact case-sensitive equality while the schema does no normalization, so the same mailbox can be added repeatedly in different cases. Re-adding 'user@x.com' when 'User@x.com' is already an attendee creates a duplicate attendee row (the dedupe check misses), and the case-sensitive blacklistedGuestEmails check at line 73 sits on the same unnormalized value — every future control layered on these emails inherits the same normalization drift; the next change (e.g. seat-count checks or per-attendee limits) gets riskier because email identity is stored in inconsistent case.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the dedupe/guard logic is case-sensitive: `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)` and the blacklist check is `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` even though the blacklist is lowercased. Since neither the schema (`z.string().email()`) nor the handler normalizes emails (e.g., `toLowerCase().trim()`), the same mailbox can be added multiple times with different casing (e.g., `User@x.com` vs `user@x.com`), creating duplicate attendee rows via `createMany` and bypassing the blacklist depending on case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The authorization gate is computed but its team branch can never authorize non-owner admins because it requires isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner, collapsing the intended admin-or-owner check to owner-only; meanwhile the attendee branch grants full add-guests power on email equality alone. Fail-closed for team admins (denied despite intended access — correctness), but the effective security envelope is asymmetric: any booking attendee passes authorization with zero role verification (a bare email string match against user.email), which is the trust-the-client-adjacent surface that any future expansion of this handler (more mutations, more data returned) will silently inherit.

adjudication.rationale:
In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&`:
```ts
const isTeamAdminOrOwner =
  (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) &&
  (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0));
```
This collapses an intended “admin OR owner” authorization into “admin AND owner”, so a non-owner team admin will be denied (fail-closed). The rest of the finding (attendee authorization via `booking.attendees.find(...email === user.email)`) is present, but whether that is wrong is policy-dependent; the AND/OR logic is a concrete, verifiable defect from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The authorization check combines isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner with &&, so isTeamAdminOrOwner is always false for any user (a membership has exactly one role, so no user is both admin and owner), making the team-admin path dead code. Team admins/owners who are not the booking organizer or an attendee receive FORBIDDEN ('you_do_not_have_permission') when trying to add guests to their own team's bookings, even though the code clearly intends to permit them; only the organizer and existing attendees can use the feature on team events.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&` between `isTeamAdmin(...)` and `isTeamOwner(...)`, meaning the check only passes if the user is *both* a team admin and a team owner. Given the variable name and intended permission path, this likely should be an OR; as written, a user who is only an admin or only an owner will fail the permission gate and may hit the `FORBIDDEN` branch unless they are also the organizer or an existing attendee.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Email-send failures are caught and reduced to console.log('Error sending AddGuestsEmails') while the mutation returns { message: 'Guests added' }. When sendAddGuestsEmails fails (SMTP outage, renderEmail throw, unbounded replyTo rejection), the organizer and all attendees receive no notification and no updated ICS, yet the user sees the 'Guests added' success toast — the failure is completely invisible to the user and unobservable beyond a server console line with no error object logged.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is wrapped in a `try/catch` that swallows all errors and only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` without logging the error object, while the mutation still returns success (`{ message: "Guests added" }`) and the UI shows a success toast on `onSuccess`. This is a diff-grounded observability/UX issue (email notification failure becomes invisible), but the core mutation (DB update + `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`) still succeeds, so it’s not a strictly verifiable correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The error-toast fallback showToast(message || t('unable_to_add_guests')) is dead code because message is a template literal `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}` that is always a non-empty (truthy) string. The 'Unable to add guests' fallback can never render; when err.data?.code is undefined the user literally sees a toast beginning with 'undefined: ', and t() on a non-translation-key message renders raw internal error text, so the intended friendly fallback is unreachable.

adjudication.rationale: In `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` the `onError` handler builds `message` as a template literal: ``const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`;`` and then calls `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")`. A template literal always produces a (truthy) string, even when `err.data?.code` is `undefined`, resulting in a toast like `"undefined: ..."`. Therefore the `unable_to_add_guests` fallback is effectively unreachable as the finding states, and users can see unfriendly/incorrect error text introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The attendee rows are committed via prisma.booking.update (line 92) before eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees runs (line 168) with no transaction and no rollback, so a calendar failure returns an error after the DB write has already persisted. If updateCalendarAttendees throws (calendar API outage, credential not valid for the referenced calendar), the user sees an error toast and keeps the dialog open believing nothing happened, but the guests are already persisted; on retry the dedupe filter removes all guests and the mutation returns the misleading BAD_REQUEST 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' instead of completing — the calendar event never gets the new attendees and the user is told the emails are invalid.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the DB write happens via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is called, and there is no transaction/rollback around these steps. Since `updateCalendarAttendees` is not wrapped in a try/catch (only email sending is), any calendar/API failure will throw after the attendees have already been persisted. On the client, `onSuccess` is the only place that closes the dialog/resets state, so an error leaves the dialog open implying nothing changed. A retry will fetch the booking with the newly persisted attendees and `uniqueGuests` becomes empty (filtered out by `booking.attendees.some(...)`), causing a `BAD_REQUEST` with message `emails_must_be_unique_valid`, matching the described misleading behavior and leaving the external calendar unsynced.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: booking.userId || 0 } }) throws an unhandled Prisma error when booking.userId is null, surfacing as a tRPC INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500). Bookings without an owning user (booking.userId null) that are otherwise actionable by an attendee produce a raw 500 instead of the 4xx the caller-facing contract implies, and the error propagates before any useful validation message is returned.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `addGuestsHandler` (`packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts`), the organizer lookup uses `prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: booking.userId || 0 } })`. If `booking.userId` is `null`/`undefined` (which the `|| 0` suggests is possible), this will query `id: 0` and `findFirstOrThrow` will throw a Prisma exception (not a `TRPCError`). There is no surrounding handling to map this to a 4xx, so it will surface as a tRPC internal 500 before returning any caller-friendly validation error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The server schema accepts duplicate emails in the guests array (no uniqueness refine and no case normalization), so a direct API call with ['a@x.com','a@x.com'] creates duplicate attendee rows via createMany. Duplicate attendee records are persisted and each duplicate receives its own copy of the ICS/notification email; the only uniqueness enforcement lives in the client-side dialog schema, which is trivially bypassed by any non-UI caller.

adjudication.rationale: The server-side ZAddGuestsInputSchema only validates email format (z.array(z.string().email())) and does not enforce uniqueness or normalize case. In addGuests.handler.ts, `uniqueGuests` filters only against *existing* `booking.attendees` and the blacklist, not against duplicates within `guests`, so an input like ['a@x.com','a@x.com'] will produce duplicate entries in `guestsFullDetails` and be persisted via `attendees.createMany`. Additionally, `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` uses the original (possibly duplicated) `guests`, and the event’s attendees list can include duplicates, causing multiple notification/ICS emails to the same address. Client-side uniqueness refine in AddGuestsDialog is bypassable by direct API calls.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Both the already-attendee dedupe (guest === attendee.email) and the blacklist check (blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)) are case-sensitive while the blacklist entries are lowercased but the incoming guest is not normalized. Submitting 'Foo@Bar.com' when 'foo@bar.com' is already an attendee creates a duplicate attendee row, and any blacklisted email submitted with non-lowercase casing silently bypasses the BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS blocklist entirely.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `blacklistedGuestEmails` are lowercased (`.map((email) => email.toLowerCase())`) but the filter compares with the raw `guest` string: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`, so a blacklisted email with different casing can bypass the blocklist. The attendee dedupe is also case-sensitive: `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)`, allowing duplicates like `Foo@Bar.com` vs `foo@bar.com` if the stored attendee email casing differs. The diff shows no normalization (e.g., `.toLowerCase()`) on incoming `guests` before these checks.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The guests array has no maximum length (z.array(z.string().email()) with no .max()), so a single mutation can create an unbounded number of attendee rows and trigger an unbounded email fan-out. One authenticated request with thousands of emails inserts thousands of attendee rows and fans out thousands of outbound emails plus a calendar update in a single synchronous request path — unbounded storage growth and request amplification on the user-facing mutation path, with no cap anywhere in the handler either.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts`, `guests` is defined as `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.max(...)` cap. The handler `addGuestsHandler` (`addGuests.handler.ts`) then `createMany` inserts one attendee row per entry in `uniqueGuests` and calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, which constructs a `Promise` per attendee (and additional organizer/team-member emails) in `sendAddGuestsEmails` (`packages/emails/email-manager.ts`) and awaits `Promise.all`. This makes the user-facing mutation path susceptible to unbounded row creation and email fan-out (plus `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`) in a single request, enabling request amplification/abuse and unbounded storage growth.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The EventManager is constructed from getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) — the invoking user's credentials — even though the handler already loaded booking.user.credentials (lines 35-39) and the calendar event being updated belongs to the booking organizer. When an attendee or team admin (both authorized by the permission check) triggers addGuests, updateCalendarAttendees runs against the wrong person's calendar account: it either throws (turning the mutation into a 500 after attendees were persisted) or silently operates on the wrong calendar, so the organizer's calendar event never gains the new attendees.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the booking is loaded with `user.credentials` (organizer) included, but `EventManager` is instantiated with `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (the *invoking* user): `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user); const eventManager = new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] });` and then `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is called. Since the permission check explicitly allows non-organizers (attendees or team admin/owner) to invoke this mutation, the calendar update will run with the wrong account’s credentials and may fail or update the wrong calendar. The diff also shows attendees are persisted via `prisma.booking.update(...createMany...)` before the calendar update, so a failure would leave DB changes applied without calendar updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The replyTo header is built by appending every attendee email (organizer plus all attendees) with no bound, and this list grows cumulatively every time guests are added to the booking. Repeated use of the add-guests feature on a popular booking grows the organizer notification's replyTo header without limit until the sending mail provider rejects it — at which point the failure is swallowed by the handler's catch (console.log only), so attendees silently stop receiving any notifications.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/emails/templates/organizer-add-guests-email.ts`, the organizer email builds `replyTo` as `[organizerEmail, ...this.calEvent.attendees.map(({ email }) => email)]` with no cap, so as `addGuests` repeatedly appends attendees (see `addGuests.handler.ts` updating `attendees.createMany` and then building `evt.attendees` from all booking attendees), the `replyTo` header can grow without bound. Additionally, `addGuests.handler.ts` wraps `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` in a `try/catch` that only `console.log`s on failure and does not surface the error, meaning notification sending failures (including from oversized headers) are silently swallowed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Guests silently dropped by the filter (already attendees, or blacklisted) are never reported back — the API returns success for the survivors with no indication of which requested guests were skipped. A user who pastes a list where some emails are already attendees sees 'Guests added' and has no way to know part of their input was discarded; if they later re-submit the dropped ones expecting clarity, they hit the misleading 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' error instead of an explanation.

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuestsHandler` the server silently filters out requested guests that are already attendees or blacklisted (`uniqueGuests = guests.filter(...)`), but still returns success (`return { message: "Guests added" }`) with no info about skipped emails. Worse, when all requested emails are filtered out (`uniqueGuests.length === 0`), it throws `BAD_REQUEST` with message `"emails_must_be_unique_valid"`, which is misleading because the failure can be due to "already an attendee" or "blacklisted" rather than invalid/non-unique emails. This is the classic parallel hand-maintained pair — the next validation change (e.g., a max-length cap on the server per the unbounded-array issue) will be applied to one copy and silently not the other, leaving client and server disagreeing about what input is accepted.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/components/dialog/AddGuestsDialog.tsx`, the client defines its own `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` as `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(...)` (uniqueness) and uses it to validate `multiEmailValue` before calling `trpc.viewer.bookings.addGuests`. This is a diff-grounded, maintainability/consistency issue: client/server validation rules already differ and are maintained in parallel, which can lead to disagreements about accepted input as the API evolves (even if it doesn't currently prove a runtime failure from this diff alone).
